evidenceChecked: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook section 3.1.3.5 and glossary entries for factor, response, control group, randomization, and DOE confounding
Haas et al., In Vivo Assay Guidelines sections 2.3.1 and 3.1.2–3.1.4
Fumo-dos-Santos and Ferreira, Dealing with confounding in observational studies, definition and mediator comparison

findings.finding: The manifest declares scene-clinical-wrap-up to contain no material claims, but content/05-clinical-wrap-up.md teaches and applies the lesson's central evidence-dependent definitions: independent and dependent variables, controlled variables versus control conditions, the three-part confounder test, and positive- and negative-control functions. Repetition or application in a transfer scene does not make those claims non-material. The scene is consequently omitted from the relevant claims.json scene mappings and has no same-scene source note, leaving its central scientific teaching without the required traceable evidence bridge.
findings.resolution: Set scene-clinical-wrap-up to claims-mapped; add that scene ID to claim-variable-roles, claim-confounder-ambiguity, and claim-control-functions; and add a learner-visible source note naming every source supporting those claims. Map any additional retained material claim as appropriate. Keep the diabetes-specific causal details explicitly stipulated as fictional assumptions, or separately source and map them if presented as real-world facts.

findings.finding: The attribution record identifies the lesson as version 0.1.1, while lesson.json and all structured pack artifacts identify the reviewed candidate as version 0.2.0. This makes the attribution identity stale for the frozen candidate.
findings.resolution: Change the stated attribution version to 0.2.0 and confirm that the rest of the attribution text describes this candidate version.

findings.finding: The NIST bullet says that NIST supports 'confounding,' but references.json correctly records that NIST section 5.7 uses confounding only in the design-of-experiments aliasing sense and is not cited for the third-variable sense taught in this lesson. The lesson's third-variable and mediator distinction is instead supported by source-confounding-observational, with the assay guidance supplying related extraneous-variable context. The attribution wording therefore blurs a material source-scope boundary that the structured records otherwise handle correctly.
findings.resolution: Limit the NIST bullet to factors, responses, and controlled or uncontrolled inputs, or explicitly identify its different DOE-aliasing sense. Attribute the lesson's third-variable confounder and causal-pathway exclusion to Fumo-dos-Santos and Ferreira.

findings.finding: The keyed interpretation is academically correct: the near-zero negative control supplies the expected baseline, while the failed known-target positive control means the detector has not demonstrated response capability and therefore prevents treating the unknown zero as evidence of target absence. The integrated transfer item likewise requires all three confounder checks and does not reward the false shortcut that any uncontrolled difference is automatically a confounder.

limitations: The requested scope excluded site/, so the graph record for topic-scientific-inquiry-variables-controls, the prerequisite graph relationship, and the course terminology ledger were not independently inspected. Outcome existence and cross-lesson terminology continuity therefore remain unverified in this run.

The direct PMC article route initially returned a reCAPTCHA page. The cited confounder definition, mediator boundary, bibliographic identity, and article context were still checked through publicly accessible PMC search indexing, PubMed, and SciELO records.

Repository-wide automated validation and source-preflight commands were not run because the requested scope prohibited inspecting scripts/ and site/. The frozen pack itself was read completely and the academic verdict does not depend on validator success.
This review assesses general scientific-methods accuracy rather than clinical-care validity. The diabetes scene was judged only as an explicitly fictional, non-advisory role-identification exercise.
